clinicalPearls: A difficult airway describes difficulty with mask ventilation, supraglottic device placement, laryngoscopy, intubation, or surgical airway access, and may be anticipated or unexpected

Preoperative assessment combines several predictors (mouth opening, Mallampati class, thyromental distance, neck mobility, prognathism, prior difficulty, and pathology) since no single test is reliable
A structured plan with pre-formulated backup steps and clear failure criteria is essential, and progression through a difficult-airway algorithm should be deliberate and time-limited
Preoxygenation and apnoeic oxygenation extend safe apnoea time and are central to preventing hypoxic injury
When intubation fails, the priority shifts from securing the tube to maintaining oxygenation using face mask or supraglottic devices
A can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate situation is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate front-of-neck access (cricothyroidotomy) without delay
For a known or predicted difficult airway, an awake technique with a flexible bronchoscope preserves spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes
Limiting repeated laryngoscopy attempts reduces trauma, bleeding, and oedema that can convert a difficult airway into an impossible one; documentation and patient alerting are vital afterwards
reference.pathophysiology: Airway difficulty arises from anatomical or pathological factors that impair alignment of the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes or obstruct airflow. Congenital syndromes, obesity, limited neck extension, restricted mouth opening, tumours, infection, trauma, previous surgery, radiation, and airway oedema all contribute. Under anaesthesia, loss of muscle tone can collapse the pharynx and worsen obstruction. When ventilation and oxygenation fail, progressive hypoxaemia leads within minutes to bradycardia, hypoxic brain injury, cardiac arrest, and death, so oxygenation rather than intubation is the overriding physiological goal.
additionalDifferentials: Airway foreign body or obstructing tumour
Airway oedema from angioedema or infection
Oesophageal intubation mistaken for a difficult airway
additionalInvestigations: Bedside airway assessment scores and examination of relevant pathology
Nasendoscopy or flexible airway endoscopy to evaluate obstructing lesions
Imaging (radiograph, CT) to characterise airway anatomy and masses when indicated
Capnography to confirm tracheal placement and ventilation
Review of previous anaesthetic records and airway alerts
redFlags: Can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate scenario requiring immediate front-of-neck access
Progressive desaturation despite optimal mask and supraglottic ventilation
Rapidly worsening airway obstruction from oedema, bleeding, or an expanding mass
Repeated failed attempts causing trauma, bleeding, and deteriorating airway conditions
reference.prognosis: Most anticipated difficult airways are managed safely with planning and appropriate techniques; unanticipated failure with delayed rescue oxygenation can cause hypoxic brain injury or death within minutes.
pitfalls: Persisting with repeated intubation attempts instead of prioritising oxygenation
Failing to declare and act on a can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate emergency in time
Not preparing backup equipment and a clear stepwise plan in advance
Failing to document the difficulty and alert the patient for future anaesthetics
management: Optimise oxygenation throughout with preoxygenation and apnoeic oxygenation to extend safe apnoea time
Formulate a structured, time-limited airway plan with pre-defined backup steps and clear failure criteria before induction
For an anticipated difficult airway, consider awake tracheal intubation with flexible endoscopy while spontaneous ventilation is preserved
When intubation fails, prioritise oxygenation using a face mask or supraglottic airway device rather than repeated laryngoscopy attempts
Declare and act on a can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate emergency with immediate front-of-neck access by cricothyroidotomy
Confirm tracheal placement and adequacy of ventilation with continuous capnography
Document the difficulty, issue an airway alert, and involve senior anaesthetic and surgical airway support early
